title: Operating Iceberg tables
summary: The maintenance and layout work that keeps Iceberg tables fast and cheap: compaction, snapshot expiry, orphan cleanup, sort orders and monitoring with metadata tables.

blocks.text: An Iceberg table that nobody maintains gets slower and more expensive every day. Immutable files and snapshots (chapter 22) mean nothing is ever cleaned up implicitly. Some managed catalogs and platforms run maintenance for you; with open-source engines it is your job. Procedures below are Spark `CALL` procedures in a catalog named `lake`; check the current documentation for argument names in your version.
25.1 Why tables degrade

head: Symptom
Cause
Fix
rows: Streaming or frequent micro-batch commits, high write parallelism, over-partitioning
Thousands of small manifests, huge metadata.json with many snapshots
Accumulated delete files in merge-on-read tables
Storage bill grows faster than data
Unexpired snapshots keep deleted files alive; orphan files from failed writes
Data not clustered on filter columns
Sort order, sort or z-order compaction

blocks.text: 25.2 Compaction: rewrite_data_files

Compaction reads groups of small files (and their delete files) and writes fewer, larger files close to the target size, then commits a `replace` snapshot. Readers are unaffected: they see either the old files or the new ones. Strategy `binpack` only combines files; `sort` also reorders rows by the table's sort order or an explicit one, including `zorder(...)` for multi-column clustering.

blocks.title: Spark SQL: compaction
blocks.text:
-- bin-pack recent partitions only
CALL lake.system.rewrite_data_files(
  table   => 'sales.orders',
  where   => 'order_ts >= TIMESTAMP "2026-11-10 00:00:00"',
  options => map('target-file-size-bytes', '536870912',
                 'partial-progress.enabled', 'true'));

-- cluster on two filter columns
CALL lake.system.rewrite_data_files(
  table      => 'sales.orders',
  strategy   => 'sort',
  sort_order => 'zorder(customer_id, product_id)');

items: **Target size**: the default `write.target-file-size-bytes` is 512 MB. Files of roughly 128 MB to 1 GB balance parallelism and per-file overhead; very selective point lookups may prefer smaller files.
**Scope**: compact only partitions that changed (`where`). Rewriting a whole multi-TB table every night is the most common maintenance waste.
**Partial progress** commits file groups as they finish, so a long job does not lose everything on one conflict and conflicts with concurrent writers are smaller.
**Conflicts**: compaction is a writer. With merge-on-read tables receiving deletes, it can conflict with the delete commits; schedule it away from heavy write windows or limit it to cold partitions.

blocks.text: 25.3 Snapshots, manifests and orphans

blocks.title: Spark SQL: cleanup procedures

items: **expire_snapshots** removes snapshots from metadata and deletes data, delete and manifest files no longer reachable from any remaining snapshot or ref. It defines your time-travel window: expire after 7 days and you cannot time travel 8 days back. Tags with their own retention survive. Table properties such as `history.expire.max-snapshot-age-ms` set defaults.
**rewrite_manifests** regroups manifest entries so manifests align with partitions and are fewer and larger, which speeds planning.

**remove_orphan_files** lists the table location and deletes files that no metadata references, typically left by failed or retried writes. It must only touch files older than any in-flight write; use a generous `older_than` (days, not minutes) and run `dry_run` first.

blocks.text: Running `remove_orphan_files` with a short `older_than` while a writer is mid-commit deletes files the writer is about to reference, corrupting the table. Also make sure the table location is not shared with other tables or tools: everything unreferenced under it is considered an orphan.
25.4 Write-time layout: distribution and sort order
The cheapest compaction is the one you avoid by writing well. Two table-level settings shape writes from Spark:

items: **Distribution mode** (`write.distribution-mode`): `none` writes whatever each task holds (many small files per partition); `hash` shuffles rows by partition so each partition is written by few tasks; `range` range-partitions by sort order, needed for good global sorting. Defaults have changed across versions; set it explicitly.
**Sort order**: declared in metadata and used by writers and sort compaction.

blocks.title: Spark SQL: declared write order

blocks.text: Linear sort helps the first sort column most. Z-order interleaves bits of several columns so each gets partial clustering; it helps when queries filter on any of two or three columns, at higher compaction cost. Neither helps columns that are not filtered.
25.5 Monitoring with metadata tables
Every Iceberg table exposes metadata tables queryable with SQL: `snapshots`, `history`, `files`, `manifests`, `partitions`, `entries`, `refs` and more. They are the basis of table health dashboards.

blocks.title: Spark SQL: health queries
blocks.text:
-- small-file report per partition
SELECT partition, count(*) AS files,
       round(avg(file_size_in_bytes) / 1048576) AS avg_mb
FROM lake.sales.orders.files
GROUP BY partition
HAVING count(*) > 50 AND avg(file_size_in_bytes) < 64 * 1048576;

-- commit rate and operations over the last day
SELECT operation, count(*) AS commits
FROM lake.sales.orders.snapshots
WHERE committed_at > current_timestamp() - INTERVAL 1 DAY
GROUP BY operation;

-- planning pressure
SELECT count(*) AS manifests, sum(added_data_files_count) AS added
FROM lake.sales.orders.manifests;

items: Track per table: data file count and average size, delete file count, manifest count, snapshot count, metadata.json size, commit rate and commit failures.
Alert on trends, not single values: a delete-file count that doubles weekly means compaction is not keeping up.

blocks.text: 25.6 Streaming writers and small files

A streaming writer commits on every checkpoint (Flink) or trigger (Spark Structured Streaming). Each commit produces at least one file per writing task per partition touched. With a 30-second checkpoint, 8 writer tasks and 4 active partitions, that is up to 32 files every 30 seconds, about 92,000 files a day, most of them a few MB.

Lengthen the commit interval to the latency the business actually needs. Moving from 30 seconds to 5 minutes cuts files and snapshots by 10x. Hash-distribute by partition so each partition gets one writer, and keep compaction away from partitions still being written.

blocks.title: Maintenance as a platform service
blocks.text: A platform team runs about 2,000 Iceberg tables. Instead of each pipeline scheduling its own maintenance, a nightly job reads metadata tables for every table, scores them (small files, delete files, manifests, snapshot age) and runs only the procedures needed, with per-table overrides in a config file.
items: Compute for maintenance dropped by about half compared with blanket nightly compaction.
Snapshot retention is set per data class: 7 days by default, longer via tags for regulated tables.

blocks.title: Write a maintenance policy
blocks.text: Design maintenance for a Flink CDC table (merge-on-read, equality deletes, 3-minute commits, 4 TB, partitioned by day) that analysts query in Trino with a 2-second dashboard target. Specify which procedures run, how often, on which partitions, and which metrics trigger them, and explain how you avoid conflicts with the Flink writer.
hints: Which costs grow fastest: data files, delete files, or snapshots?
How long must the time-travel window be, and who decides?
What older_than value is safe for orphan cleanup with this writer?

items: Iceberg never cleans up implicitly; unmaintained tables slow down and grow storage.
rewrite_data_files compacts and can sort or z-order; scope it to changed partitions.
expire_snapshots sets the time-travel window and frees storage; rewrite_manifests speeds planning.
remove_orphan_files needs a generous age threshold and a dry run first.
Distribution mode and sort order at write time prevent much of the compaction work.
Metadata tables (files, snapshots, manifests) are the basis for monitoring and policy-driven maintenance.

blocks.q: Storage keeps growing although a nightly job deletes old rows. What is the most likely reason?
options: Snapshots are not expired, so files removed from the current snapshot are still referenced by older ones
Delete commits immediately remove files, so storage cannot grow
blocks.explain: A DELETE only removes files from the new snapshot. Old snapshots still reference them until expire_snapshots runs and deletes unreachable files.

blocks.q: Why is a short older_than on remove_orphan_files dangerous?
options: It deletes snapshots needed for time travel
It can delete files written by an in-flight commit that are not yet referenced by metadata
blocks.explain: Files from a commit in progress are unreferenced until the swap succeeds. Snapshot expiry, not orphan removal, affects time travel.

blocks.q: Queries filter on either customer_id or product_id, never on both. Which layout is most appropriate?
blocks.explain: Z-order gives both columns partial clustering, so either filter can prune. A linear sort mainly helps its first column, and identity partitioning on a high-cardinality key creates huge numbers of tiny partitions.

blocks.q: A Spark job writes a partitioned table with distribution mode `none` and 400 tasks. What is the typical result?
options: Up to 400 small files in every partition the job touches
Files exactly at the target size
An error, because partitioned writes need range distribution
blocks.explain: With no shuffle, each task writes its own file for every partition it holds rows for. Hash distribution groups rows by partition first so few tasks write each partition.
